item.title: QE ArXiv Watch: Week of October 05 - October 12, 2026
item.description:
# QE ArXiv Watch Weekly Week ending October 12, 2026

What if your experiment could stop early, keep its error guarantees while you peek at the results, and still estimate effects precisely? One paper this week gets close—and it points to a broader theme across the batch: good design can do more than improve precision. It can make inference faster, more reliable, and easier to operationalize.

Yu et al. build a method for multifactor online experiments that combines treatment allocation, continuous monitoring, and estimation. Their block-orthogonal designs separate treatment information from nuisance block effects, while an anytime-valid e-value lets teams monitor evidence without invalidating their test by checking repeatedly. In simulations, the procedure stopped after an average of 1.4 batches, versus 7.7 for a safe-testing competitor, and had lower treatment-effect estimation error. In a 128-response prompt experiment, it stopped at batch four while the alternatives ran to the end. The practical draw is especially clear when experiments are expensive: orthogonal arrays can also cut a seven-factor design from 128 runs to 16 while preserving the design’s key properties. The reported type-I error was 5.8%, so—as always with a new procedure—teams should check how its guarantees and operating characteristics fit their own setting.

For causal experiments with complicated assignment schemes, Klosin et al. offer a refreshingly practical variance estimator. Their connected-components approach uses the pattern of which potential outcomes can’t be observed together to build an unbiased estimate of an upper bound on design-based variance. It reduces to familiar estimators under complete and cluster randomization, but can be much sharper in more tangled designs. In a school-network application, it gave the shortest standard error in seven of eight specifications; some competing calculations took hours, while theirs took under a second. If your treatment assignments are dependent—because of networks, geography, or other design constraints—this looks worth a closer read.

Two cautions from Zaidi et al. are useful for anyone running online tests on skewed outcomes. Blocking on a pre-experiment scale measure reduced variance in their simulations, with finer blocks producing larger gains. But handling the tails matters: within-block winsorization improved precision while maintaining coverage in a tail-effect scenario, whereas global winsorization and inverse-variance weighting produced badly calibrated results. The latter is a good reminder that a tiny standard error is no comfort if the analysis has quietly changed the estimand.

The remaining papers extend the design conversation in different directions. Yin et al. ask how far mobile sensors must move when the signal model changes. Their certification method can bound movement when the model perturbation is small and the placement objective has enough separation; the key message is that perturbation size alone won’t guarantee stability. Liu et al. show, theoretically, that LinUCB’s adaptive sampling can approach D-optimal designs in a small-gap regime—suggesting an algorithm built for regret reduction can also be information-efficient.

Across this week’s work, design is increasingly treated as part of inference, not just a setup step. The question for practitioners: where could a better allocation—or a better account of dependence—save more than just sample size?

Featured Papers This Week

  • Klosin et al.: Simple Standard Errors for Complicated (Quasi-)Experimental Designs (DOE)
  • Zaidi et al.: On the Benefit of Blocking for Online Experiments with Skewed Data (DOE)
  • Yin et al.: Movement Stability of D-Optimal Sensor Placement Under Projector Perturbations (DOE)
  • Yu et al.: Design-Driven Inference for Online Experiments: Jointly Optimal Evidence Collection, Testing, and Estimation (DOE)
  • Liu et al.: Sampling Allocation of LinUCB: Optimal Design Limits in the Small-Gap Regime (DOE)
